title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical PHP cyber-security update issued
description: International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of
body: International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon. Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix. "These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities."We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance, external" without specifying the reason.The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet. Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language.OpenAI said in a blog post, external that the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms.The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered."Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.  It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale.The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes."Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external.Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning, external."PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said. "The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was, external "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

schema.headline: Websites taken down worldwide as critical PHP cyber-security update issued

title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
description: After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackda
body: After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund.A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go? It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time."The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said."If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth. The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's. "Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era. The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories. Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund. Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic. It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future. While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that. Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

schema.headline: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built

title: UK City of Culture: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for 2029
description: The four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations
body: The four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations to be the next UK City of CultureBySteven McIntosh and Ian YoungsBlackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029. The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.The shortlisted cities are:Image source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot.What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of."She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen."Milton KeynesImage source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie.What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side".Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond."SheffieldImage source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? The traditional centre of steel and cutlery manufacturing, Sheffield has since become known for musical exports like the Arctic Monkeys and Pulp, for its annual documentary film festival, and for the Crucible - one of the leading theatres outside London.What have they said? The city's bid put its spotlight on Sheffield's "world-renowned creative heritage, as well as our ambitious future plans".Celebrating its place on the shortlist, councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said: "Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit... Culture is part of who we are."WrexhamImage source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? North Wales's largest city was a powerhouse of the industrial revolution, and most recently hit the headlines when its historic football club Wrexham AFC was bought by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.What have they said? The bid said: "Our ambition is simple but bold: to make Wrexham the world's most playful place."Joanna Knight OBE, chair of the Wrexham bid, styled as Wrecsam2029, explained: "There's a real sense that something very special is happening here. Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean... the opportunities are enormous."

schema.headline: UK City of Culture: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for 2029

title: Bruno Fernandes rounds on Michael Carrick after Man Utd lose to Como in Champions League
description: Figure caption, Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on CarrickByManchester United reporter in ComoManchester United captain Bruno Ferna
body: Figure caption, Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on CarrickByManchester United reporter in ComoManchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards."It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."Figure caption, 'That is on the manager' - Fernandes on Man Utd tacticsCarrick avoids questions on future, apologises to fans for unacceptable displayCarrick also refused to answer questions about his own future.Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility."I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable."I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over."It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them."I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them."Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all."Figure caption, Carrick responds to Fernandes criticism on tacticsSeven without a win - Man Utd's bleak pictureAfter winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract.However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland.Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015.Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time.The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D.It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent.They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford.Figure caption, Carrick 'bitterly disappointed' by Man Utd peformanceWhat happens now?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick acknowledges the club's fans after the 4-1 defeat by ComoUnited flew straight back to Manchester after the game.It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled. Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada."There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch."It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times."I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can."Figure caption, Man Utd fans on if Carrick should stayFollow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

schema.headline: Bruno Fernandes rounds on Michael Carrick after Man Utd lose to Como in Champions League

title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the S
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on WednesdayByJames CookScotland editor and Graeme EssonBBC ScotlandThe UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear"."The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.The timeline of Jackdaw and RosebankThe UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences."We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.Image caption, The Jackdaw platform is located east of AberdeenScotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland."It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.Figure caption, Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial?But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.Image source, EPAImage caption, Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morningJackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.Image caption, BBC News visited the Jackdaw platform this summerLabour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.On the Front Line: Inside the PlatformAn inside look at Jackdaw, the UK’s newest and most contested gas platform.

schema.headline: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences

title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia EditorReporting fromMoscowAfter two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard."In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace."I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said,  "but things are moving in that direction."All rather vague.It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken holdIn recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader."Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says."Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?""Of course!"A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe."Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace

title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
description: A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.It will
body: A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART."We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC."My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life."But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me."Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something"."Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back."Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father died from Alzheimer's last month, said he knew how it felt to lose a loved one to dementia, and had seen first-hand the devastating impact of the disease on families."That's why I'm proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible," he said.The AD-SMART study is what's known as a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial where several treatments are tested simultaneously, with the results compared with one group of participants taking a placebo or dummy.This means those involved have a higher likelihood of getting an active treatment than in a traditional trial.If any drug isn't showing benefit it can be dropped quickly and a new treatment added in its place - the approach has been used successfully in cancer and motor neurone disease.The two initial drugs being tested are metformin, used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, for ADHD, which were selected by an international panel of experts.Both drugs may help reduce brain inflammation, which is a driver of neurodegeneration, said chief investigator Prof Paresh Malhotra, group leader at the UK Dementia Research Institute Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London."For too long, Alzheimer's research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer - sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we've found something that works," he told the BBC."We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer's disease."For the drugs to be successful, the study has to show that they have beneficial effects on thinking and the ability to carry out everyday activities."That's what patients and their carers care about," said Prof Malhotra.Some 1,200 participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer's will be recruited at more than 30 sites across the UK. Sites in Cambridgeshire, Surrey, London, Southampton and Edinburgh are already open.Scientists expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030 and, in that time, additional treatments are likely to be added.All the participants will have regular health checks including cognitive tests, which will help researchers assess how effective the treatments are.Angela Bucksey's husband Steve, who is her study partner, told the BBC: "Joining the trial has brought us back from the despair of a diagnosis which everybody recognises is non-recoverable."People who know we are on a drug trial understand that we're doing something about it and, rather than be sorry for us, they can be encouraging."Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer's Research UK said "time is precious" for people living with Alzheimer's disease and more treatment options are urgently needed.People with a confirmed Alzheimer's diagnosis who would like to take part can register their interest on the AD-SMART website, external.The trial is being led by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK.Partners include the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Medical Research Council and Health Data Research UK, with funding by UK government.

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian citiesByJa
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian citiesByJaroslav LukivUkraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday. It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed. Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war. Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St PetersburgSpeaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line."We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.  Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.Image source, Truth SocialImage caption, Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for UkraineBefore the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release. When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. "Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

title: South Africa vs Australia: Tourists facing defeat after remarkable day with careers on the line
description: Second Test, Gqeberha (day four of five)South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81Australia 99 & 156-4: Head 87*; Rabada 2-30Australia
body: Second Test, Gqeberha (day four of five)South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81Australia 99 & 156-4: Head 87*; Rabada 2-30Australia trail by 170 runsScorecardNot since the Nottingham Ashes Test in 2005, Shane Warne's spin and watching Ashley Giles' leg glance from behind a cushion, had Australia been asked to follow-on in an away Test.It had only happened to them on one other occasion anywhere in the world in 38 years.But by being bowled out for 99 by South Africa in their first innings of the second Test, Australia matched those lows and handed their hosts an unlikely route to winning this Test and leveling the series.Travis Head remains on 87 not out, but this was a calamitous day for the tourists as they conceded their biggest first-innings lead since 1984, before failing for the second time in the same day's play.At 156-4 in their second innings they are still 170 runs behind and the Proteas now look likely winners with a day to go."There are a number of players playing for their careers in this innings," said former Australia opener Simon Katich, Australia's highest scorer from that Trent Bridge Test 21 years ago, on SEN Radio.For some, it might even be too late...If Katich's words seem strong for a side 1-0 up in the series, this South African subsidence was the latest example of an Australian batting line-up only consistent for its inconsistency.Bowled out for 132 in the first Test of the Ashes last winter, they piled up 511 in Brisbane in the next.They scored 567 at the end of the Ashes, but were bundled out for 198 by Bangladesh in their next Test en route to a shock defeat.Even the highs of Matt Renshaw's 190 in the first-Test win in Durban were countered by the fact no other Australian made 50.And after another failure, Marnus Labuschagne appears the most at risk. He will not get another chance to bat for his place before Cape Town hosts the third Test from 27 October.After edging a drive to third slip for 14 off Anrich Nortje in the morning, he gave it away by hitting spinner Simon Harmer to long-on after tea for 39 - his third dismissal in the thirties in the series. It was made worse by the fact he had only survived an lbw decision on review just three runs earlier. It is now 47 innings since the 32-year-old, once the leading batter in the world, has made a Test century. "Only he knows what was going through his mind when he tried to take Harmer down the ground, against the breeze, when Australia are trying to play for a draw," added Katich."How will the Australian selectors view that dismissal? "He's been given plenty of rope over the past few years, when plenty of others haven't, but he has."Australia head coach Andrew McDonald said he was "disappointed" with Labuschagne's dismissal. "You saw what we saw," he said. "For me, the option is there if the ball is the right area. It is a strength of this, but in that scenario there probably are some shots that players would take back. "He did a lot of hard work once again. I feel like I am on repeat around the amount of 30s that he has got. That has become a danger period for him. "We had a good partnership going and were starting to claw ourselves back into the game, albeit a long way behind. "When you do that hard work you've got to cash in and unfortunately that wasn't to be the case for Marn. We were disappointed and he will be too."Opener Nic Maddinson is another who must simply await his fate. He was not involved in the Wednesday-morning collapse, but only because he had already edged Kagiso Rabada to slip the night before.Opening the batting against Rabada and Marco Jansen would be feverishly difficult for a regular opener, never mind a batter more used to the middle order. It is because of that very fact Maddinson has chased balls outside off stump in both innings, leaving the left-hander with two ducks to go with scores of eight and 48 since his surprise recall aged 34.As he watched on, Sam Konstas, once seen as Australia's next opener, made 151 not out for New South Wales back home.Credit must also go to left-armer Jansen, who was superb in taking 5-33 in Australia's first innings.He was in full flow when dismissing Renshaw, Alex Carey and Beau Webster to rip out the middle order - all three were caught between wicketkeeper and gully.Renshaw and wicketkeeper Carey have credit in the bank, but Webster, who became the day's 13th wicket when he was pinned lbw by Harmer in the final 20 minutes, will be another looking over his shoulder.An admirable cricketer, he averages 34.13 with the bat and 28.75 with the ball in his 11 completed Tests. But he has also now gone seven innings without a 50 since the Ashes and yet to reach three figures.McDonald said Australia know they are not the "perfect batting unit" and he could not defend some of the dismissals. "We've had some of these moments across the journey," he said. "The pitch didn't play too many tricks either, there was a bit of bounce. "You do have to give some credit to the South Africans, they exposed some of our deficiencies, but there was some batter error there."I think we are better than that but as we sit here now, I can't defend that."

title: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
description: Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to
body: Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.The tougher sanctions, due to come into effect next year, build on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years for contempt of court.The move is the latest bid to push killers to attend court, with the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) acknowledging that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter them if they are already behind bars."Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said."Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences", she added. The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, social visits could be banned for nearly a month and any prison privileges revoked for longer. Judges will also being able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for almost three months for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing. For criminals aged 18-20, judges will be able to impose similar restrictions but for shorter periods of time, the MoJ said.However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions. But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves". The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa, law graduate Zara Aleena and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa have previously advocated for changes to the laws. All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings. Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said the announcement follows "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice". She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

title: Bukayo Saka's injury 'does not look good at all' - Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta
description: Mikel Arteta says the quadriceps injury Arsenal's Bukayo Saka picked up in the 2-2 Champions League draw against Bayern Munich "does not look good at
body: Mikel Arteta says the quadriceps injury Arsenal's Bukayo Saka picked up in the 2-2 Champions League draw against Bayern Munich "does not look good at all".The 25-year-old winger went down in the 10th minute at Allianz Arena - attempting to play a pass with nobody around him - and had to be replaced by Eberechi Eze, who went on to score the opening goal."They are a bit concerned. A player who has to come off with a really sharp pain is never good news but we have to wait and see," Arteta told TNT Sports.Saka has had fitness issues in recent months and his game time was managed at the end of last season, as well as with England at the World Cup, because of an Achilles injury he picked up in March.He missed the March international break and seven games for the Gunners, but returned to help them lift the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years.Saka started the Champions League final defeat by Paris St-Germain but was substituted after 54 minutes, and only started three of England's eight games at the World Cup - scoring a hat-trick in the 6-4 third-place win over France.The forward also had surgery on a hamstring injury he picked up in December 2024, which kept him out for 101 days in the 2024-25 season.He made 49 appearances as Arsenal won the title last term, despite a stop-start season - as well as the Achilles issue, he pulled out of the warm-up against Leeds with a hip injury in January and a hamstring problem kept him out for about four weeks.But he remains vital to the Gunners, whose win percentage is notably more impressive with him in the team.Despite the loss of Saka early on in the game, Arsenal still produced a good performance and could have won the match late on after Declan Rice's late equaliser. "The only negative is seeing one of their star players, Saka, having to pull up with an injury early in the first half," said Champions League Match of the Day pundit Nedum Onuoha."He was lying on the floor with his hand up and he knew he was in a bit of trouble, so now the concern will be how long he is out for."It's not necessarily something that means the team will struggle heavily, but there is a reason why he is regarded as one of the best players in this Arsenal team and is seen as being important for them."After Saka's withdrawal Noni Madueke, who had started on the left wing, switched to the right and looked bright, while Eze scored the opening goal from the left after coming off the bench. "This is one of the reasons their squad has been built the way it has been and I think Madueke and Eze did well on the wings today after Saka came off," added Onuoha."In terms of options, at this moment in time for Arsenal, it is not going to be an issue - they will miss the star power that he has, they still have plenty of other wide players who can step up and do the job while they wait for him to come back."Arsenal's style of play has been criticised this season but, even before Saka's withdrawal, the Gunners played on the front foot and enjoyed more possession than their German opponents. Losing Saka, who has scored four goals in 11 appearances in all competitions, will be tough to deal with. But the Gunners have invested heavily in their squad over the past two summer transfer windows and have options. Madueke can play on both wings, while summer signing Christos Tzolis - although currently out with a hamstring injury - has started the season well. The Gunners also have 16-year-old Max Dowman as an attacking option, and the youngster has already shown that he can have an impact for the senior side after scoring in the Premier League last season. Arteta, who was asked what the rest of the forward line will need to do in Saka's absence, said he was pleased with what he saw against Bayern. "I think Ebs [Eze] had a great game. Not only the ball, but the actions. His overall performance, I think his commitment without the ball as well," he said."And when the other ones come in, I think they really contributed to this. First of all, the energy. "And then to bring different tools that the team needed in that moment to get something out of the game. So, very pleased again."

title: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds
description: Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research.A Cambrid
body: Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research.A Cambridge study found that of the 86 scientists named by UK exam boards, the English chemist, whose work in the 1950s helped reveal the structure of DNA, was the only woman.Exam specifications set out the skills and knowledge students are expected to have gained by the end of their course and how they will be assessed.Exam boards said there was "a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications".Academics from the University of Cambridge, along with institutions in the US and Australia, examined how many women were mentioned in specifications for biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, geology and astronomy.Their work, published in the British Educational Research Journal, looked at six exam boards in the UK:AQACambridge OCRPearson EdexcelWJECCCEAQualifications ScotlandAt Key Stage 4 and equivalent, including GCSEs and National 5s in Scotland, Franklin was the only woman among the 86 scientists mentioned.She was also one of three women mentioned at Key Stage 5 and equivalent - including A-levels, AS-levels, National Highers and National Advanced Highers - out of a total of 181 scientists.Marie Tharp, an American cartographer who created the first map of the floor of the Atlantic ocean in the 1950s, and Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist who discovered the existence of the Earth's inner core in the 1930s, both feature in the Cambridge OCR's A-­level Geology.Franklin, who was named in Cambridge OCR's GCSE Biology and Scottish Highers Biology, produced a famous DNA image known as Photograph 51.Cambridge scientists Francis Crick and James Watson used the image to work out the following year that DNA has a double-helix structure.Watson, Crick and Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery. Franklin had died four years earlier.Academics who wrote the paper found that "several major scientific breakthroughs" in specifications were made by women, but they were not explicitly mentioned.The paper said: "Many of the scientific discoveries and explanations were developed in the 1800s and early 1900s, a period when scientific and mathematical practice was largely, but not solely, dominated by men. "Our findings confirm that the UK science specifications reflect this historical imbalance: although women made significant contributions to major scientific breakthroughs, this fact is rarely acknowledged."The academics recommended that Franklin should be included "in all specifications when teaching DNA structure".They also said specifications should refer to Marie Curie, who discovered radium and polonium and coined the term radioactivity, and nuclear physicist Lise Meitner, who discovered nuclear fission, among others.Stephanie Buttigieg, one of the authors, said: "Relatable role models can help keep more girls in STEM by strengthening their sense of belonging in science and fostering positive attitudes towards scientific careers."A spokeswoman for the Joint Council for Qualifications, which represents AQA, Cambridge OCR, CCEA, WJEC and Pearson, said: "Exam boards recognise that there is a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications, and this is an area they will be focusing on as these qualifications are reformed."Qualifications Scotland said the Curriculum Improvement Cycle offered "an opportunity to consider gender representation within our future qualifications and assessments". The Department for Education in England said "girls should see the contribution women have made in STEM", adding it was "committed to improving the school curriculum over the coming years, and as part of that will make sure every girl can see where their learning can take them".The Scottish Government said it was "committed to closing the gender gap in STEM and will carefully consider the findings of this research".Additional reporting by Marthe de Ferrer and Rahib Khan

schema.headline: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds

title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick JacksonMarco Silva an
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick JacksonMarco Silva and Thomas CopelandBBC Verify French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the  riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.   The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools. Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders... "We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France. "When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country.""Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.         BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

schema.headline: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain

title: Glee reboot: The US high school musical comedy-drama is to return on Hulu and Disney+
description: We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.Ryan Murphy's series, wh
body: We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015.The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club.The reboot was announced, external by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday.The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health.In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance.Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester.The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences.In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film.Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances.On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again"."I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said. Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think so… It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break. "I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things."In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, co-creator Murphy confirmed he had written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan.He also said he had "been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members"."It's very sweet, they all had a lot of questions but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea," he said. "Nobody's read it, so we'll see."He added: "I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, because we were very close when we were making it."It came after Michelle, who played Rachel Berry, the ambitious singer at the centre of the club, had told E! News that she - like Lynch - would be more than happy to return."I will always love Glee," she said. "I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me... I will follow Ryan wherever he goes."Speaking to Bustle recently, another star of the show, Chris Colfer, admitted that any such reboot would be difficult following the death of Naya Rivera, who played Glee club favourite Santana Lopez."It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya is gone," said Colfer, who portrayed Kurt Hummel - the flamboyant singer and original choir member who faces bullying at the school."But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don't know, but hopefully I'll have more information and I can actually think about it."Rivera died in 2020 at the age of 33 in an accidental drowning.Hers was the third death among the Glee cast. Monteith, who played football star turned singer Finn Hudson, died in 2013 at the age of 31 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.Mark Salling, another Glee cast member, took his own life in 2018 at the age of 35 while awaiting sentencing on child pornography charges.A mini Glee reunion occurred on Sunday at London's Royal Albert Hall, when Darren Criss, aka Glee's Blaine Anderson, brought out Colfer for a duet of the song Baby It's Cold Outside.Earlier this month, former Glee co-stars Harry Shum Jr and Amber Riley reunited on Dancing with the Stars.

schema.headline: Glee reboot: The US high school musical comedy-drama is to return on Hulu and Disney+
